input_text: Al-Tabari gathered the opinions of the generations before him. Some said Ee-rahm was a city: Alexandria, according to one early authority; Damascus, according to another. But the view al-Tabari preferred was simpler. The ee-maad, he argued, were the poles of tents. Aa-d were people of poles: travellers, moving with the rains and the pasture. And he added a sentence that cuts to the heart of this mystery. No building of theirs with columns, he wrote, is known through any authentic report. The search later led to Shisr, a small oasis in Dhofar, about one hundred and seventy kilometres inland, with a Bedouin well and a ruined fort that earlier travellers had dismissed as only a few centuries old. Perhaps that is the real lesson of Ee-rahm. A people can survive in memory long after their stones are gone, or even if they never built in stone at all. A few words in a sacred text have outlived empires, maps and explorers.
